text: Why do I get butterflies when I'm nervous?

steps.title: The alarm goes off
steps.say: As an example, say something makes you nervous at 21:15. Your brain's threat centre fires down nerves to your adrenal glands, which pour adrenaline into your blood within seconds.

composed.caption: Threat signal triggers adrenaline release
composed.basis: Textbook sympathetic stress response (Cannon's fight-or-flight); amounts are illustration

steps.title: Blood is sent to battle stations
steps.say: Adrenaline speeds your heart and squeezes the vessels to your gut, steering blood toward muscles in case you must run. Digestion is treated as optional right now.

steps.title: Your stomach stalls
steps.say: With less blood and nerve signals telling it to pause, your stomach churns your pizza along more slowly. It empties noticeably slower during the nervous spell.

steps.title: This is the flutter
steps.say: The gut wall's muscle twitches irregularly and its vessels tighten. Gut nerves report these odd sensations to your brain, which you feel as fluttering butterflies.

composed.caption: Tight gut vessels, twitching muscle, nerves report
composed.basis: Gut-brain axis and visceral sensation (Mayer, Nat Rev Neurosci 2011); amounts are illustration

steps.title: It passes
steps.say: Once the moment is over, adrenaline clears within minutes, your heart slows, and blood flows back to your gut so digestion resumes.

lines.text: Nerves trigger adrenaline, which pulls blood away from your gut and sends it toward your muscles.
Your stomach slows down and twitches, and gut nerves report that as fluttering.
In the example your heart goes from about 78 to 91, then settles afterwards.
